```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(nbzinbPate)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = "center", out.width = "85%")

# Saved results of inst/benchmark/benchmark.R and simulation.R. Look in the
# installed package first, then in the source tree (when rendering from the
# repository before re-installing).
result_file <- function(name) {
  p <- system.file("benchmark", "results", name, package = "nbzinbPate")
  if (p == "") p <- file.path("..", "..", "inst", "benchmark", "results", name)
  p
}
bm  <- readRDS(result_file("benchmark.rds"))
sim <- readRDS(result_file("simulation.rds"))

# Formatting helpers
sci  <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 1)
f2   <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
f3   <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
# "IRR (lower, upper)" or "OR (lower, upper)" from a 95% Wald interval
wald <- function(est, se) {
  sprintf("%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)", exp(est), exp(est - qnorm(0.975) * se),
          exp(est + qnorm(0.975) * se))
}
# Percentage change implied by a log-scale coefficient, e.g. "22% more"
pct <- function(est, more = "more", fewer = "fewer") {
  p <- round(100 * (exp(est) - 1))
  if (p >= 0) paste0(p, "% ", more) else paste0(-p, "% ", fewer)
}

# Benchmark summaries used in the text
max_diff <- function(model, q) {
  max(sapply(c("bioChemists", "NMES1988"), function(ds) {
    a <- bm[[ds]][[model]]$agreement
    a$max_abs_diff[a$quantity == q]
  }))
}
all_pass <- all(sapply(c("bioChemists", "NMES1988"), function(ds)
  all(bm[[ds]]$NB$agreement$pass) && all(bm[[ds]]$ZINB$agreement$pass)))
```

# Introduction

Many outcomes in health, the social sciences and industry are counts: the
number of doctor visits in a year, of articles a student publishes, of
defects on a production line. The Poisson regression model is the natural
starting point, but it forces the variance to equal the mean. Real count data
are often **overdispersed**, with a variance much larger than the mean, and
can also contain **more zeros** than a Poisson model with the same mean can
produce. Ignoring overdispersion gives standard errors that are too small, and
ignoring excess zeros gives a poor description of who has a zero count and why.

The negative binomial (NB2) model handles overdispersion by adding a
dispersion parameter $\theta$, so that
$\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mu+\mu^2/\theta$. The zero-inflated negative binomial
(ZINB) model goes further and treats the data as coming from two processes: a
*structural* process that produces zeros only (for example, people who never
see a doctor), and an NB count process that can also produce zeros.

The goal of this project is an R package, **nbzinbPate**, that fits both
models with estimation code written from scratch. The NB model is fitted by
iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) for the regression coefficients,
alternated with Newton-Raphson for $\log\theta$. The ZINB model, whose
likelihood is not that of a generalized linear model, is fitted by an EM
algorithm whose M-steps are IRLS fits. No general-purpose optimizer
(`optim()`, `nlm()`, ...) and no GLM fitter (`glm()`, `lm()`, ...) is used.
The package is checked against `MASS::glm.nb()` and
`pscl::zeroinfl()`, studied in a simulation, and applied to physician office
visits in the NMES1988 data.

# Methods

## Models

**NB2.** For counts $Y_i$ with covariates $x_i$ and offset $o_i$,
$$
P(Y_i = y) = \frac{\Gamma(y+\theta)}{\Gamma(\theta)\, y!}
  \left(\frac{\theta}{\theta+\mu_i}\right)^{\theta}
  \left(\frac{\mu_i}{\theta+\mu_i}\right)^{y},
\qquad \log\mu_i = x_i^\top\beta + o_i,
$$
so that $E(Y_i)=\mu_i$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Y_i)=\mu_i+\mu_i^2/\theta$. As
$\theta\to\infty$ the model reduces to the Poisson.

**ZINB.** With probability $\pi_i$, where $\mathrm{logit}\,\pi_i = z_i^\top\gamma$,
observation $i$ is a structural zero; otherwise it comes from
$\mathrm{NB}(\mu_i,\theta)$:
$$
P(Y_i=0)=\pi_i+(1-\pi_i)f_{NB}(0;\mu_i,\theta),\qquad
P(Y_i=y)=(1-\pi_i)f_{NB}(y;\mu_i,\theta),\ y\ge 1,
$$
where $f_{NB}(0;\mu,\theta)=\{\theta/(\theta+\mu)\}^\theta$. The observed-data
log-likelihood is
$$
\ell(\beta,\gamma,\theta)=\sum_{y_i=0}\log\!\big[\pi_i+(1-\pi_i)f_{NB}(0;\mu_i,\theta)\big]
+\sum_{y_i>0}\big[\log(1-\pi_i)+\log f_{NB}(y_i;\mu_i,\theta)\big].
$$
Because every zero contributes the log of a *sum*, $\ell$ is not the
log-likelihood of an exponential-family GLM, and IRLS cannot be applied to it
directly.

## NB: IRLS for $\beta$ alternated with Newton-Raphson for $\log\theta$

**IRLS with $\theta$ fixed.** For the log link, $\partial\mu/\partial\eta=\mu$,
and $V(\mu)=\mu+\mu^2/\theta$. Fisher scoring is then a weighted least-squares
regression of a working response $z$ on $X$:
$$
w_i = a_i\frac{(\partial\mu_i/\partial\eta_i)^2}{V(\mu_i)}=a_i\frac{\theta\mu_i}{\theta+\mu_i},\qquad
z_i = (\eta_i-o_i)+\frac{y_i-\mu_i}{\mu_i},\qquad
\beta^{(t+1)}=(X^\top WX)^{-1}X^\top Wz ,
$$
where $a_i$ are prior weights ($a_i=1$ for an ordinary fit). Each update is
solved by a QR decomposition of $W^{1/2}X$, which avoids forming $X^\top WX$
and squaring its condition number.

**Newton-Raphson with $\beta$ fixed.** The score and second derivative of
$\ell$ in $\theta$ are
$$
U(\theta)=\sum_i a_i\Big[\psi(y_i+\theta)-\psi(\theta)+\log\theta+1-\log(\theta+\mu_i)-\frac{y_i+\theta}{\theta+\mu_i}\Big],
$$
$$
H(\theta)=\sum_i a_i\Big[\psi'(y_i+\theta)-\psi'(\theta)+\frac1\theta-\frac{2}{\theta+\mu_i}+\frac{y_i+\theta}{(\theta+\mu_i)^2}\Big],
$$
with $\psi$ and $\psi'$ the digamma and trigamma functions. The update is done
on $\phi=\log\theta$, which keeps $\theta>0$; by the chain rule
$$
U_\phi=\theta U,\qquad H_\phi=\theta^2H+\theta U,\qquad \phi\leftarrow\phi-U_\phi/H_\phi .
$$

**Outer loop.** The fit starts from a Poisson IRLS fit for $\beta$ (the same
IRLS code with $\theta=\infty$, so $w_i=a_i\mu_i$) and the moment estimate
$\theta_0=\sum_i a_i/\sum_i a_i(y_i/\mu_i-1)^2$, then alternates the two steps,
warm-starting each one at the current values.

**Standard errors.** At convergence,
$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta)=(X^\top\hat WX)^{-1}$, treating $\theta$ as
known as `glm.nb()` does, and $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\theta)=\{-H(\hat\theta)\}^{-1/2}$.

## ZINB: EM with IRLS M-steps

Let $D_i=1$ if observation $i$ is a structural zero. If the $D_i$ were
observed, the complete-data log-likelihood would split into a logistic
regression for $D_i$ and a weighted NB regression with weights $1-D_i$, each
of which IRLS can fit. EM replaces $D_i$ by its conditional expectation.

**E-step.** The posterior probability of a structural zero is
$$
\tau_i=\frac{\pi_i}{\pi_i+(1-\pi_i)f_{NB}(0;\mu_i,\theta)}\ \ (y_i=0),\qquad \tau_i=0\ \ (y_i>0).
$$

**M-step, zero part.** Maximize $\sum_i[\tau_i\log\pi_i+(1-\tau_i)\log(1-\pi_i)]$
over $\gamma$: a logistic regression with fractional response $\tau_i$,
fitted by IRLS with $w_i=\pi_i(1-\pi_i)$ and
$z_i=z_i^\top\gamma+(\tau_i-\pi_i)/\{\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\}$. Because the logit is
the canonical link, this IRLS is exact Newton-Raphson.

**M-step, count part.** Maximize $\sum_i(1-\tau_i)\log f_{NB}(y_i;\mu_i,\theta)$
over $(\beta,\theta)$. This is exactly the NB fit above with prior weights
$a_i=1-\tau_i$, so the same code is reused.

Both M-steps are run to convergence, warm-started at the previous values. EM
starts from the NB fit for $(\beta,\theta)$ and a logistic IRLS fit of
$I(y_i=0)$ for $\gamma$. Each M-step increases the expected complete-data
log-likelihood, which guarantees that $\ell$ never decreases (Dempster, Laird
and Rubin, 1977); the code checks this at every iteration.

## Standard errors for ZINB: analytic Hessian

EM does not produce standard errors, so after convergence the observed
information of $\ell$ with respect to $(\beta,\gamma,\log\theta)$ is computed
analytically and inverted. Writing $\eta^z_i=z_i^\top\gamma$,
$\eta^c_i=x_i^\top\beta+o_i$, $\ell^f_i=\log f_{NB}(y_i;\mu_i,\theta)$ and
$a,b\in\{\eta^c,\phi\}$, the derivatives simplify when expressed through
$\tau_i$:
$$
\frac{\partial\ell_i}{\partial\eta^z_i}=\tau_i-\pi_i,\qquad
\frac{\partial\ell_i}{\partial a}=(1-\tau_i)\frac{\partial\ell^f_i}{\partial a},
$$
$$
\frac{\partial^2\ell_i}{\partial(\eta^z_i)^2}=\tau_i(1-\tau_i)-\pi_i(1-\pi_i),\quad
\frac{\partial^2\ell_i}{\partial\eta^z_i\,\partial a}=-\tau_i(1-\tau_i)\frac{\partial\ell^f_i}{\partial a},
$$
$$
\frac{\partial^2\ell_i}{\partial a\,\partial b}=(1-\tau_i)\frac{\partial^2\ell^f_i}{\partial a\,\partial b}
+\tau_i(1-\tau_i)\frac{\partial\ell^f_i}{\partial a}\frac{\partial\ell^f_i}{\partial b}.
$$
These are Louis' (1982) formula: the observed information equals the expected
complete-data information minus the variance of the complete-data score, and
$\tau_i(1-\tau_i)=\mathrm{Var}(D_i\mid y_i)$ is the "missing information". The
NB derivatives $\partial\ell^f_i/\partial\eta^c_i=\theta(y_i-\mu_i)/(\theta+\mu_i)$,
$\partial^2\ell^f_i/\partial(\eta^c_i)^2=-\theta\mu_i(\theta+y_i)/(\theta+\mu_i)^2$,
$\partial^2\ell^f_i/\partial\eta^c_i\partial\phi=\theta\mu_i(y_i-\mu_i)/(\theta+\mu_i)^2$,
and the $\phi$ derivatives $\theta U_i$ and $\theta U_i+\theta^2H_i$ come from
Section 2.2. The chain rule ($\partial\eta^c_i/\partial\beta=x_i$,
$\partial\eta^z_i/\partial\gamma=z_i$) assembles the full Hessian $H$, and
$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta,\hat\gamma,\log\hat\theta)=\{-H\}^{-1}$. The
standard error of $\hat\theta$ follows from the delta method,
$\mathrm{SE}(\hat\theta)=\hat\theta\,\mathrm{SE}(\log\hat\theta)$.

## Convergence criteria and numerical safeguards

The inner IRLS loops stop when no coefficient changes by more than
$10^{-10}$, and the Newton loop when $|\Delta\phi|<10^{-10}$. A criterion on
the parameters is needed because the log-likelihood is flat at its maximum: a
change in $\ell$ of $10^{-7}$ can leave $\beta$ wrong in the sixth digit, and
the NB log link is not canonical, so Fisher scoring converges only linearly.
The NB outer loop stops when $\ell$ changes by less than $10^{-8}$ *and* the
parameters by less than $10^{-8}$; EM stops when $\ell$ changes by less than
$10^{-8}$ and the parameters by less than $10^{-6}$.

Each IRLS or Newton step is halved if it lowers the log-likelihood by more
than rounding error which means it passed the maximum. The steps are halved until the maximum is not passed. Probabilities are handled on the log scale
(`plogis(eta, log.p = TRUE)` and a log-sum-exp form of
$\log[\pi+(1-\pi)f_{NB}(0)]$), so $\pi_i$ is never rounded to exactly 0 or 1.
Two boundary cases are detected and reported with a warning: $\hat\theta$
diverging to $\infty$ (no overdispersion; $\theta$ is capped at $10^8$), and
all $\hat\pi_i\to 0$ in the ZINB model (no zero inflation, so the zero-model
coefficients diverge to $-\infty$).

# The R package

The package exports two fitting functions, two control functions, and a full
set of S3 methods for each fitted class.

| Function | Purpose |
|:---|:---|
| `nbreg(formula, data, offset, control)` | NB2 regression: IRLS + Newton-Raphson for $\log\theta$ |
| `zinbreg(formula, data, offset, control)` | ZINB regression by EM; formula `y ~ x | z` |
| `nbreg_control()`, `zinbreg_control()` | tolerances, iteration limits, `trace` |
| S3 methods (both classes) | `print`, `summary`, `coef`, `vcov`, `logLik`, `AIC`/`BIC`, `fitted`, `residuals`, `nobs`, `predict` |

**Design.** Each model has a formula interface (`nbreg()`, `zinbreg()`) that
builds the design matrices, checks the input and packages the result, and a
matrix-level engine (`nbreg_fit()`, `zinbreg_fit()`) that only does the
estimation. This separation is what makes the EM count-part M-step a single
call to `nbreg_fit()` with prior weights $1-\tau_i$ and a warm start. The
two-part formula `y ~ x | z` is split in base R: a formula is a call, and
because `|` binds more loosely than `+`, its right-hand side is a call to `|`
whose two arguments are the count and zero parts. Without `|`, the same
covariates are used in both parts, as in `zeroinfl()`. Offsets may be given
as an argument or as `offset()` terms in the (count) formula. The only
dependency is base R's **stats** package.

**Methods.** `logLik()` returns an object carrying the number of parameters
and observations, so `AIC()` and `BIC()` work. `residuals()` returns response
or Pearson residuals; for ZINB the Pearson residuals use
$\mathrm{Var}(Y_i)=(1-\pi_i)\mu_i\{1+\mu_i(\pi_i+1/\theta)\}$. `predict()`
accepts `newdata` (using the fitted factor levels, contrasts and offset) and,
for ZINB, `type = "response"` ($(1-\pi)\mu$), `"count"` ($\mu$) or `"zero"`
($\pi$).

**Testing.** The `testthat` suite compares both functions with
`glm.nb()` and `zeroinfl()` at the project tolerances on both data sets,
checks the analytic score and Hessian against numerical derivatives, checks
that EM never decreases $\ell$, tests offsets, single-covariate and
intercept-only models, the boundary cases and informative errors, and
verifies that no function in the package calls a prohibited optimizer or
fitter. `R CMD check` passes with no errors, warnings or notes on Windows,
macOS and Linux through GitHub Actions. The package is installed with
`devtools::install_github("brandonp8/nbzinbPate")`; Section 6.2 shows it in
use, and the README has a further example.

# Benchmarking

Both functions were compared with the reference implementations on
`pscl::bioChemists` and `AER::NMES1988`, using the reference functions with
tight tolerances (`glm.control(epsilon = 1e-10)` and
`zeroinfl.control(reltol = 1e-12)`). The script is
`inst/benchmark/benchmark.R`.

```{r bench-table}
bench <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("bioChemists", "NMES1988"), function(ds) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("NB", "ZINB"), function(m) {
    r <- bm[[ds]][[m]]
    a <- setNames(r$agreement$max_abs_diff, r$agreement$quantity)
    data.frame(Data = ds, Model = m,
               Coef. = sci(a[["Coefficients"]]),
               SE = sci(a[["Standard errors"]]),
               `theta / log theta` = sci(a[[3]]),
               logLik = sci(a[["Log-likelihood"]]),
               `Ours (s)` = sprintf("%.2f", r$time[["ours"]]),
               `Ref. (s)` = sprintf("%.2f", r$time[["reference"]]),
               Iter. = r$iterations, check.names = FALSE)
  }))
}))
knitr::kable(bench, booktabs = TRUE, align = "llllllrrr",
             caption = paste("Maximum absolute difference from MASS::glm.nb()",
                             "(NB) and pscl::zeroinfl() (ZINB), median time,",
                             "and number of outer (NB) or EM (ZINB) iterations.",
                             "Required: at most 1e-5 (NB coefficients and SEs),",
                             "1e-4 (NB theta, logLik), 1e-3 (all ZINB)."))
```

All quantities `r if (all_pass) "meet" else "do NOT all meet"` the required
tolerances, by a wide margin. For NB, the coefficients, standard errors,
$\theta$ and log-likelihood agree with `glm.nb()` to within
`r sci(max(max_diff("NB", "Coefficients"), max_diff("NB", "Standard errors"), max_diff("NB", "theta"), max_diff("NB", "Log-likelihood")))`,
essentially machine precision. (The only slightly larger difference is in
$\mathrm{SE}(\hat\theta)$, about
`r sci(max(sapply(c("bioChemists", "NMES1988"), function(ds) { t <- bm[[ds]]$NB$table; t$abs_diff[t$quantity == "SE(theta)"] })))`:
`MASS::theta.ml()` evaluates the information at the $\theta$ value before its
final Newton step, while `nbreg()` evaluates it at $\hat\theta$.) For ZINB the
largest difference in any coefficient or standard error is
`r sci(max(max_diff("ZINB", "Coefficients"), max_diff("ZINB", "Standard errors")))`,
and the log-likelihoods agree to
`r sci(max_diff("ZINB", "Log-likelihood"))`. On NMES1988 our ZINB
log-likelihood is `r if (bm$NMES1988$ZINB$loglik_higher) "slightly higher" else "not higher"`
than that of `zeroinfl()`. The complete side-by-side estimates are in the
Appendix.

The NB fits take about as long as `glm.nb()`. The ZINB fits are
`r round(min(bm$bioChemists$ZINB$time[["ours"]] / bm$bioChemists$ZINB$time[["reference"]], bm$NMES1988$ZINB$time[["ours"]] / bm$NMES1988$ZINB$time[["reference"]]))`
to
`r round(max(bm$bioChemists$ZINB$time[["ours"]] / bm$bioChemists$ZINB$time[["reference"]], bm$NMES1988$ZINB$time[["ours"]] / bm$NMES1988$ZINB$time[["reference"]]))`
times slower than `zeroinfl()`. This is expected. `zeroinfl()` updates all
parameters jointly with a quasi-Newton method (BFGS), which converges
superlinearly, whereas EM converges linearly at a rate set by the fraction of
missing information. The zero component is weakly identified in
bioChemists, so EM needs `r bm$bioChemists$ZINB$iterations` iterations there,
against `r bm$NMES1988$ZINB$iterations` for the larger NMES1988 data. In
addition, every M-step is a fully converged weighted NB fit.

# Simulation study

```{r sim-numbers}
#| include: false
ss <- sim$summary
bias_mcse <- abs(ss$bias) / (ss$mc_sd / sqrt(sim$design$R))   # bias in MC SEs
zero_rows <- grepl("^zero_", ss$parameter)
```

To check that `zinbreg()` recovers known parameters and that its standard
errors are accurate, $R=`r sim$design$R`$ data sets of size
$n=`r sim$design$n`$ were simulated (seed `r sim$design$seed`, script
`inst/benchmark/simulation.R`) from
$\log\mu_i=`r sim$design$beta[1]` + `r sim$design$beta[2]`\,x_{1i} `r sim$design$beta[3]`\,x_{2i}$
with $x_1\sim N(0,1)$ and $x_2\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(0.5)$,
$\mathrm{logit}\,\pi_i=`r sim$design$gamma[1]` + `r sim$design$gamma[2]`\,z_{1i}$
with $z_1\sim N(0,1)$, and $\theta=`r sim$design$theta`$. Covariates were
redrawn for each data set. On average about
`r round(100 * mean(sim$diagnostics$prop_zero[["Mean"]]))`% of each
simulated sample were zeros.

```{r sim-table}
st <- sim$summary
names(st) <- c("Parameter", "True", "Mean est.", "Bias", "MC SD",
               "Mean SE", "SE / MC SD", "Coverage")
knitr::kable(st, booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3,
             caption = paste("Simulation results: bias, Monte Carlo SD versus",
                             "mean estimated SE, and empirical coverage of",
                             "95% Wald intervals (theta on the log scale)."))
```

All `r sim$diagnostics$n_converged` fits converged, with
`r sim$diagnostics$n_boundary` boundary cases and no warnings. The estimates
are essentially unbiased: every bias is within
`r f2(max(bias_mcse))` Monte Carlo standard errors of zero (the Monte Carlo
SE of a mean estimate is $\mathrm{SD}/\sqrt{R}$). The ratio of the mean
estimated SE to the Monte Carlo SD ranges from `r f2(min(ss$se_ratio))` to
`r f2(max(ss$se_ratio))`. With $R=`r sim$design$R`$, an SD is itself estimated
with a relative error of about $1/\sqrt{2(R-1)}\approx
`r round(100 / sqrt(2 * (sim$design$R - 1)))`$%, so these ratios are
consistent with 1. The empirical coverage of the 95% Wald intervals ranges
from `r f2(min(ss$coverage))` to `r f2(max(ss$coverage))`, all within two
Monte Carlo standard errors
($\pm 2\times`r f3(sim$diagnostics$coverage_mcse)`$) of 0.95. This also
provides an independent check of the analytic Hessian: errors in the second
derivatives would show up as SE ratios far from 1. The standardized errors
in the figure below are centred at 0 with roughly unit spread.

The only visible pattern is that the zero-part SEs are somewhat smaller than
the Monte Carlo SDs (ratios `r f2(min(ss$se_ratio[zero_rows]))` and
`r f2(max(ss$se_ratio[zero_rows]))`), while the count-part SEs are slightly
larger. With $R=`r sim$design$R`$ these deviations are not statistically
significant, but a slight underestimation of uncertainty in the weakly
identified zero component at $n=`r sim$design$n`$ is plausible.

```{r sim-figure}
#| fig-cap: "Standardized errors (estimate - truth) / SE across the 100 replications. Under correct SEs these are approximately N(0, 1); dashed lines at +/-1.96."
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-width: 7
truth <- setNames(sim$summary$true, sim$summary$parameter)
zstd  <- sweep(sim$estimates, 2, truth) / sim$std_errors
op <- par(mar = c(8, 4, 1, 1))   # wide bottom margin for the rotated labels
boxplot(zstd, las = 2, cex.axis = 0.75, ylab = "(estimate - truth) / SE",
        col = "grey85")
abline(h = 0)
abline(h = c(-1.96, 1.96), lty = 2)
par(op)
```

# Data analysis: NMES1988

The NMES1988 data (Deb and Trivedi, 1997; available in the **AER** package)
record the number of physician office visits (`visits`) for 4,406
individuals aged 66 and over in the US National Medical Expenditure Survey,
1987-88. The covariates used are the number of hospital stays (`hospital`),
self-perceived health (`health`: poor, average or excellent), the number of
chronic conditions (`chronic`), `gender`, years of education (`school`), and
whether the individual has private insurance (`insurance`).

```{r nmes-data}
data("NMES1988", package = "AER")
d <- NMES1988
y <- d$visits
```

## Descriptive summary

```{r nmes-describe}
desc <- data.frame(
  n = length(y), Mean = mean(y), Variance = var(y),
  `Var./mean` = var(y) / mean(y),
  `Zeros` = sum(y == 0),
  `Prop. zero` = mean(y == 0),
  `Poisson P(0)` = dpois(0, mean(y)),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(desc, booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3,
             caption = paste("Physician office visits in NMES1988. Poisson",
                             "P(0): probability of a zero under a Poisson",
                             "distribution with the sample mean."))
```

The number of visits ranges from 0 to `r max(y)`, with mean
`r f2(mean(y))` and variance `r f2(var(y))`: the variance is
`r round(var(y) / mean(y), 1)` times the mean, far from the equality the
Poisson model requires. There are also many more zeros than a Poisson
distribution allows: `r sum(y == 0)` individuals
(`r round(100 * mean(y == 0), 1)`%) made no office visit, while a Poisson
distribution with the same mean gives a zero with probability
`r f3(dpois(0, mean(y)))`, i.e. about `r round(length(y) * dpois(0, mean(y)))`
zeros. The covariates explain part of this, so the fitted models below give a
fairer comparison, but the data clearly show overdispersion and excess zeros.

## Models

```{r nmes-fit}
#| echo: true
f_count <- visits ~ hospital + health + chronic + gender + school + insurance
f_zinb  <- visits ~ hospital + health + chronic + gender + school + insurance |
  hospital + chronic + gender + school + insurance

m_pois <- glm(f_count, family = poisson, data = d)   # reference Poisson model
m_nb   <- nbreg(f_count, data = d)                     # our NB
m_zinb <- zinbreg(f_zinb, data = d)                    # our ZINB
```

The count part uses all six covariates. The zero part uses the minimum set
required by the project (all covariates except self-perceived health). The
Poisson model is fitted with `glm()` for reference only.

```{r nmes-expected}
# Expected frequency of each count k under each fitted model:
# sum over observations of the fitted P(Y_i = k).
K <- 0:30
exp_pois <- sapply(K, function(k) sum(dpois(k, fitted(m_pois))))
exp_nb   <- sapply(K, function(k) sum(dnbinom(k, size = m_nb$theta,
                                              mu = fitted(m_nb))))
pi_hat <- predict(m_zinb, type = "zero")
mu_hat <- predict(m_zinb, type = "count")
exp_zinb <- sapply(K, function(k) {
  sum((k == 0) * pi_hat +
        (1 - pi_hat) * dnbinom(k, size = m_zinb$theta, mu = mu_hat))
})
obs <- sapply(K, function(k) sum(y == k))
```

```{r nmes-freq-figure}
#| fig-cap: "Observed frequencies of office visits (bars) and frequencies expected under the fitted Poisson, NB and ZINB models, for 0-20 visits."
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-width: 7
show <- K <= 20
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
bp <- barplot(obs[show], names.arg = K[show], col = "grey85", border = "grey50",
              ylim = c(0, max(obs, exp_pois) * 1.05),
              xlab = "Number of physician office visits", ylab = "Frequency")
lines(bp, exp_pois[show], type = "b", pch = 19, col = "firebrick")
lines(bp, exp_nb[show],   type = "b", pch = 17, col = "steelblue")
lines(bp, exp_zinb[show], type = "b", pch = 15, col = "darkgreen")
legend("topright", c("Observed", "Poisson", "NB", "ZINB"),
       pch = c(22, 19, 17, 15), pt.bg = c("grey85", NA, NA, NA),
       col = c("grey50", "firebrick", "steelblue", "darkgreen"), bty = "n")
par(op)
```

## Model comparison

```{r nmes-compare}
cmp <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Poisson", "NB", "ZINB"),
  df = c(attr(logLik(m_pois), "df"), attr(logLik(m_nb), "df"),
         attr(logLik(m_zinb), "df")),
  logLik = c(logLik(m_pois), logLik(m_nb), logLik(m_zinb)),
  AIC = c(AIC(m_pois), AIC(m_nb), AIC(m_zinb)),
  BIC = c(BIC(m_pois), BIC(m_nb), BIC(m_zinb)),
  `Expected zeros` = c(exp_pois[1], exp_nb[1], exp_zinb[1]),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(cmp, booktabs = TRUE, digits = 1,
             caption = sprintf(paste("Model comparison for NMES1988",
                                     "(observed zeros = %d)."), obs[1]))
```

The Poisson model fits very poorly. It predicts only
`r round(exp_pois[1])` zeros against `r obs[1]` observed, and its
log-likelihood is `r round(logLik(m_nb) - logLik(m_pois))` units below that of
the NB model, for a single extra parameter. In the figure, it puts far too
much mass at 3-8 visits and too little at 0-2 and in the right tail.
Allowing overdispersion fixes most of this: the NB model has
$\hat\theta=`r f3(m_nb$theta)`$ (SE `r f3(m_nb$SE.theta)`), and its predicted
frequencies follow the observed ones closely from about 3 visits upward.

The NB model still **under-predicts** the zeros (`r round(exp_nb[1])`
expected against `r obs[1]` observed) and **over-predicts** single visits
(`r round(exp_nb[2])` against `r obs[2]`). The ZINB model corrects both
(`r round(exp_zinb[1])` zeros and `r round(exp_zinb[2])` single visits); it
slightly over-predicts the zeros, by `r round(exp_zinb[1] - obs[1])`. It
improves the log-likelihood by `r round(logLik(m_zinb) - logLik(m_nb), 1)`
with `r attr(logLik(m_zinb), "df") - attr(logLik(m_nb), "df")` extra
parameters, and has both the lowest AIC (`r sprintf("%.1f", AIC(m_zinb))` against
`r sprintf("%.1f", AIC(m_nb))` for NB) and the lowest BIC (`r sprintf("%.1f", BIC(m_zinb))`
against `r sprintf("%.1f", BIC(m_nb))`). Unlike the bioChemists example, where BIC
preferred the simpler NB model, here both criteria favour zero inflation.
Once the structural zeros are modelled separately, the count component is
also less overdispersed ($\hat\theta=`r f3(m_zinb$theta)`$ in the ZINB model).

## Interpretation: incidence rate ratios and odds ratios

```{r nmes-irr}
s_nb <- summary(m_nb)$coefficients
s_zc <- summary(m_zinb)$coefficients$count
s_zz <- summary(m_zinb)$coefficients$zero
keep_nb <- rownames(s_nb) != "(Intercept)"
keep_zc <- !(rownames(s_zc) %in% c("(Intercept)", "Log(theta)"))
irr <- data.frame(
  Covariate = rownames(s_nb)[keep_nb],
  `NB IRR (95% CI)` = wald(s_nb[keep_nb, 1], s_nb[keep_nb, 2]),
  `ZINB count IRR (95% CI)` = wald(s_zc[keep_zc, 1], s_zc[keep_zc, 2]),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(irr, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE, align = "lcc",
             caption = paste("Count part: incidence rate ratios with 95% Wald",
                             "intervals. The reference health category is",
                             "average (the contrasts supplied with the AER data)."))
```

```{r nmes-or}
keep_zz <- rownames(s_zz) != "(Intercept)"
or <- data.frame(
  Covariate = rownames(s_zz)[keep_zz],
  `OR (95% CI)` = wald(s_zz[keep_zz, 1], s_zz[keep_zz, 2]),
  `p-value` = format.pval(s_zz[keep_zz, 4], digits = 2, eps = 1e-4),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(or, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE, align = "lcc",
             caption = paste("ZINB zero part: odds ratios of being a",
                             "structural zero (never visiting), with 95% Wald",
                             "intervals."))
```

```{r nmes-interp}
#| include: false
b_nb <- s_nb[, 1]; b_zc <- s_zc[, 1]; g <- s_zz[, 1]; p_zz <- s_zz[, 4]
or_txt <- function(v) f2(exp(g[[v]]))
```

All effects below hold the other covariates fixed.

**NB model.** Every covariate is associated with the number of visits at the
5% level. Each additional hospital stay is associated with
`r pct(b_nb[["hospital"]])` office visits (IRR `r f2(exp(b_nb[["hospital"]]))`),
and each additional chronic condition with `r pct(b_nb[["chronic"]])`.
Compared with individuals in average health, those in poor health make
`r pct(b_nb[["healthpoor"]])` visits and those in excellent health
`r pct(b_nb[["healthexcellent"]])`. Men make `r pct(b_nb[["gendermale"]])`
visits than women, each year of education is associated with
`r pct(b_nb[["school"]])` visits, and private insurance with
`r pct(b_nb[["insuranceyes"]])`.

**ZINB model, count part.** This part describes individuals who are "at risk"
of visiting a doctor. The directions and significance of all effects match
the NB model, and the health and hospital effects are almost unchanged
(IRR `r f2(exp(b_zc[["hospital"]]))` per hospital stay;
`r f2(exp(b_zc[["healthpoor"]]))` and `r f2(exp(b_zc[["healthexcellent"]]))`
for poor and excellent health). The effects of chronic conditions
(IRR `r f2(exp(b_nb[["chronic"]]))` to `r f2(exp(b_zc[["chronic"]]))`),
insurance (`r f2(exp(b_nb[["insuranceyes"]]))` to
`r f2(exp(b_zc[["insuranceyes"]]))`) and gender
(`r f2(exp(b_nb[["gendermale"]]))` to `r f2(exp(b_zc[["gendermale"]]))`)
move toward 1, although all remain significant. In the NB model these
covariates combine two effects: whether someone sees a doctor at all, and how
often. The ZINB model separates the two, and part of their association turns
out to act through the first.

**ZINB model, zero part.** The zero part models the probability of being a
structural zero, an individual who would not visit a physician regardless.
Each additional chronic condition multiplies the odds of being such a
non-user by `r or_txt("chronic")`, a `r round(100 * (1 - exp(g[["chronic"]])))`%
reduction, and private insurance multiplies them by `r or_txt("insuranceyes")`
(`r round(100 * (1 - exp(g[["insuranceyes"]])))`% lower odds). Men have
`r or_txt("gendermale")` times the odds of women of being non-users, and each
additional year of education lowers the odds by
`r round(100 * (1 - exp(g[["school"]])))`%. Hospital stays point in the same
direction (OR `r or_txt("hospital")`), but this effect is not significant at
the 5% level (p = `r f3(p_zz[["hospital"]])`). These effects are plausible:
people with chronic conditions have a reason to see a doctor, and people with
private insurance face lower costs of doing so.

**Preferred model.** I prefer the ZINB model for these data. It has the
lowest AIC *and* BIC, it reproduces the observed numbers of zeros and single
visits much better than the NB model, and its two parts have a clear and
useful interpretation. Chronic illness, insurance, gender and education are
associated both with *whether* an elderly person sees a physician at all and
with *how often* among those who do, while the effect of hospital stays acts
mainly on how often. (Self-perceived health was included in the count part
only, so its role in non-use was not assessed.) The NB model is not wrong (all
its effects have the same signs), but it mixes these two processes, and the
comparison shows that the data support separating them.

# Discussion

The package reproduces `glm.nb()` and `zeroinfl()` to far better than the
required tolerances, using only IRLS, Newton-Raphson and EM. The simulation
confirms that the ZINB estimates are unbiased and that the analytic-Hessian
standard errors give close to nominal coverage. Several limitations remain.

* **Speed.** EM converges linearly, so `zinbreg()` is 5-15 times slower than
  `zeroinfl()`. Running each M-step to full convergence is also conservative.
  Loosening the M-step tolerance roughly halves the run time without
  changing the estimates, and EM acceleration (for example SQUAREM) could
  reduce the number of iterations further, although it needs extra
  safeguards to keep the log-likelihood monotone.
* **NB standard errors.** Following `glm.nb()`, $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta)$
  treats $\theta$ as known. Because $\beta$ and $\theta$ are asymptotically
  orthogonal in the NB2 model, this costs little, but the full observed
  information would be more exact in small samples.
* **Weak identification.** When the zero component is weakly identified
  (large zero-part SEs, as in bioChemists), EM needs many iterations and the
  Wald intervals for $\gamma$ may be somewhat too narrow, as the simulation
  hints. Profile-likelihood intervals would be more reliable there.
* **Boundary cases.** When the data show no zero inflation, the MLE of
  $\gamma$ is at $-\infty$. The package detects this and warns, but it does
  not provide a formal test of zero inflation.
* **Extensions.** Natural extensions are zero-inflated Poisson and hurdle
  models, other links for the zero part (for example the probit), prior
  weights in `zinbreg()`, offsets in the zero model, and a test comparing
  the NB and ZINB models.

# AI-use statement

Claude Code was used to generate all code and to draft the report. I gave it clear step by step instructions on how to implement the package as well as rules it must follow like not using optim() or other functions. After each step and then again after completion I double-checked its work. I had to make a few corrections to its work. For instance, at first the stopping rule for the IRLS was based on log-likelihood change which converged before beta coverged. This is because the likelihood is nearly flat at its peak and the NB IRLS algorithm converges only linearly. I corrected this by having the algorithm stop when beta itself stopped changing.
